items.title: Iranians Face Anxious Wait as Threat of Attack Looms
items.summary: The United States and Israel have drawn up plans to renew strikes against Iran, creating a sense of dread among war-weary residents.
items.full_text:
Title: Iranians Face Anxious Wait as Threat of Attack Looms - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/middleeast/iranians-face-anxious-wait-as-threat-of-attack-looms.html

Published Time: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 01:34:39 GMT

Markdown Content:
Many Iranians living in the country began the week on Saturday with anxiety and dread, closely following reports that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for another wave of attacks on Iran in the coming days or weeks.

Parents agonized over whether to send their children to school or keep them close at home. Businessmen canceled work trips to avoid getting stranded if airports closed and roads became too risky. Residents in Tehran flocked to gas stations to fill up their tanks, withdrew cash from banks and stocked up on basic food items.

Some social media influencers warned their followers to keep a low profile in the coming days, and avoid unnecessary travel. Some people said that planning for war had become a new norm and they were feeling numb, as Iran has gone through two intense periods of fighting since June 2025.

“I just told my wife not to wake up our son in the morning, and keep him home, we can decide day by day how to proceed,” said Majid, a 42-year-old businessman in Tehran, in a telephone interview. He said his wife, who works at a ministry that could become a target, planned to call in sick. Majid, like all Iranians interviewed, asked that their last name not be published because of fear of retribution.

President Trump has said he was considering an attack on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections if a diplomatic deal was not reached, insisting that Iran could not have a nuclear program. American officials said last week that the United States and Israel have devised specific [plans for renewed strikes](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/politics/us-israel-renewed-iran-strikes.html).

Mr. Trump has swayed from threatening to annihilate the country to promising to rehabilitate its economy if they reach a deal. U.S. officials have said that the president could still veto the plans, as he has done in the past.

Iranians say his unpredictable nature only adds to their agony.

Shadi, a schoolteacher in Tehran, said she planned to show up for work every day unless the government closes the schools. “But in the back of my mind I keep thinking about how I can protect my students, how to act so they are not scared, if explosions happen during school hours.”

On Feb. 28, [the United States struck an elementary school i](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/05/world/middleeast/iran-school-us-strikes-naval-base.html)n the city of Minab, killing 156 children and teachers. American officials have ascribed the school strike to a [targeting error](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/16/us/politics/us-strike-iranian-school.html) caused by outdated data.

Behnam, a 38-year-old musician in Tehran, said that he felt numb and less afraid because he has survived two rounds of fighting. “What worries me and those around me most is the lack of money and simply surviving,” he said. “Everyone is trying to find a way to make money and get by.”

Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces a tight election on Tuesday, said last week that the United States and Israel must join forces to topple Iran’s regime. The comments have raised concerns in Iran that Israel may carry out military strikes before the vote.

Image

A bazaar in Tehran on Thursday.Credit...Arash Khamooshi/Polaris for The New York Times

Negotiations have stalled between Tehran and Washington, despite a frenzy of diplomacy last week by Pakistan, Qatar and Russia. In public statements, Iranian officials have said they will not surrender to Mr. Trump’s demands about Iran’s nuclear program.

Iranians have seen their own government, from military commanders to lawmakers, make daily declarations about their intent to forcefully retaliate if attacked and set the region aflame. Hard-line supporters of the government, who are a minority of the population, hold nightly rallies chanting for escalation and revenge.U.S. officials said on Friday they had obtained intelligence that [Iran was planning to target American personnel](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/politics/security-warnings-iran-threats.html) in the region.

Yet some prominent politicians and pundits have openly called for the government to tread carefully and do all it can to avoid a military escalation, fearing more suffering, destruction and instability for Iranians.

Javad Emam from the main reformist party addressed the government [on social media last week](https://x.com/JavadEmam/status/2112787053335208068): “The responsibility for today’s decision lies with you; the cost of war will be borne by the nation.”

At least 1,900 civilians were killed in 40 days of bombardment this year, according to Iran’s Red Crescent Society. The government said damages from the war amounted to about $300 billion. The economy has been in a tailspin: Sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade have contributed to the currency plunging against the dollar, and prices for some basic foods have skyrocketed more than 200 percent.

Alireza, a 54-year-old veteran of the Iran-Iraq war who lives in the city of Kerman, said that while he did not want Iran to surrender and suffer a humiliation, he was angry at the government’s lack of transparency and inability to find a peaceful solution.

“I hope the war ends as soon as possible, because war brings nothing but death and destruction,” he said in an interview from Kerman. “People are under enormous pressure and are being crushed by the economic siege.”

items.title: Ukraine’s Feeling of Moral Whiplash at the Hands of Trump
items.summary: The United States once declared that Ukraine’s fight was the front line in a global battle for freedom. Now the Trump administration is sending money to Moscow.
items.full_text:
Title: Ukraine’s Feeling of Moral Whiplash at the Hands of Trump - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/europe/ukraine-trump.html

Published Time: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 02:04:37 GMT

Markdown Content:
On the same day President Trump told reporters that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine,” President Volodymyr Zelensky [shared a photo](https://x.com/ZelenskyyUa/status/2112225056478679118) taken moments after a Russian drone struck a Ukrainian playground.

The image showed 14-month-old Angelina, bundled up in a red jumper, her shoelaces tied in perfect bows, slumped, lifeless, in a stroller. Her face was blurred. A sprinkling of dust and debris was the only hint of her [violent end](https://x.com/DenysSienik/status/2113285832324874408).

“Her mother’s name was Inna,” Mr. Zelensky wrote. “She died in the hospital.”

The statements hours apart from the two leaders hammered home a reality: Never has the chasm between Mr. Trump’s view of the war and Ukrainians’ experience of it seemed so vast.

Mr. Trump continues to periodically lament the huge numbers of lives lost in the fighting, calling it a waste. He is trying to restart peace talks. But he has begun blaming Ukraine for his domestic political problems, and turning to Russia, the country that started the blood-soaked conflict, for a helping hand.

Ukrainians over the years have [grown largely numb](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/world/europe/trump-zelensky-diesel-energy-russia-.html) to Mr. Trump’s parroting of Russian talking points, and Kyiv has adapted after he ended donations of U.S. weaponry. But to many, Mr. Trump has crossed an irrevocable line by buying Russian diesel and suspending sanctions in what energy experts call a futile effort to bring down fuel prices before the midterm elections.

Mr. Trump, who has [cut U.S. aid to Ukraine by 99 percent](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/11/world/europe/ukraine-war-zelensky-us-trump-russia.html), is sending American money to the Kremlin — and therefore to a Russian war machine that the United Nations says is killing Ukrainian civilians at a “new horrifying level.”

With that has come a profound sense of moral whiplash for Ukraine nearly five years into its wartime roller-coaster ride with America.

Image

President Trump with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine in July in Ankara, Turkey. Mr. Trump has at times boiled the war down to a conflict between two leaders who “don’t like each other.”Credit...Doug Mills/The New York Times

Not long ago, under a different U.S. president, Joseph R. Biden Jr., the United States’ message to Ukraine was that its fight was the front line in a [global battle for freedom](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/06/30/world/europe/biden-nato-ukraine-russia.html). By holding firm, he said, Ukrainians were defending the democratic world itself.

Families buried their dead believing that, whatever the cost, they were not dying alone or in vain. At funerals and on the front, in cafes and in parks, soldiers and civilians alike often talked about fighting for a cause greater than their own self-interest.

Now, Ukrainians say, they feel betrayed. Mr. Trump does not talk about the war as a matter of right and wrong. He talks about it in starkly transactional terms.

“We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given nothing to us,” Mr. Trump said last week. “Remember that.”

Chief Sgt. Pavlo Kazarin, a writer now serving in Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, said in an interview that Ukrainians were “watching Donald Trump destroy all the reputational capital that his predecessors accumulated over recent decades, when the United States supported democracy, when the United States declared that it supported freedom, and when the United States invested in soft power to support its allies around the world.”

Mr. Trump has at times boiled the war down to a conflict between two leaders who “don’t like each other” and just need to make a deal. He has falsely blamed Mr. Zelensky for starting the war, and he recently suggested that the Ukrainian leader wanted it to continue so he could enrich himself.

What Mr. Trump does not understand, Sergeant Kazarin said, is that Russia’s goal is Ukraine’s erasure as a nation. Without this understanding, the Trump administration’s peace efforts will fail, he added.

“For Ukrainians, this war is a war for existence,” Sergeant Kazarin said.

The feeling of a world turned upside down was crystallized for many Ukrainians this past week when Mr. Trump’s peace envoy, Steve Witkoff, traveled to St. Petersburg, Russia. Mr. Witkoff praised President Vladimir V. Putin as a “[humanitarian](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/politics/russia-american-prisoner-release-stephen-hubbard-trump.html)” for releasing an American prisoner the U.S. government had deemed wrongfully detained.

Image

Rescuers carrying the body of a person killed following Russian strikes in Sloviansk, Ukraine, in July. In the first half of 2026, civilian casualties were 37 percent higher than that time period the previous year.Credit...Tyler Hicks/The New York Times

A few hours later, Russia launched a salvo of 21 ballistic missiles at Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital. Three carried cluster munitions designed to detonate in the air as they approached their targets, spreading destruction across hundreds of yards, [Mr. Zelensky said](https://x.com/ZelenskyyUa/status/2113247024518684864).

The use of cluster munitions in a city of three million people was met with silence from the White House.

“Overnight, Kyiv residents heard what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like: a brutal attack with dozens of ballistic missiles striking energy infrastructure, medical facilities, shopping centers, and residential areas,” Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, wrote on social media. “Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war,” he added.

Oleksandra Matviichuk, a Ukrainian [who won](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/10/07/world/europe/ukraine-center-for-civil-liberties-nobel-peace-prize.html) the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022 for her work at the [Center for Civil Liberties](https://ccl.org.ua/en/), a nonprofit organization, noted that civilian casualties had only increased as Mr. Trump had tried for nearly two years to reach an agreement to end the war.

“This is not what you expect from the peace negotiation,” she said. “It’s a clear indicator that something is going wrong.”

By focusing on Russia’s [territorial claims](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2025/08/16/world/trump-putin-meeting-alaska), [mineral rights](https://www.nytimes.com/article/ukraine-mineral-deal-us-trump.html) in Ukraine for the United States and other [business deals](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/us/politics/trump-russia-deals.html), with scant mention of attacks directed at civilians, the Trump administration is sending a signal to Moscow that “people have no meaning and they can do whatever they want,” Ms. Matviichuk said.

“Trump’s peace negotiations have already gone down in history as the deadliest years for Ukraine’s civilian population since the start of the full-scale invasion,” she said.

In 2025, injuries and deaths among civilians in Ukraine rose 31 percent, [according to the United Nations](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/2025-deadliest-year-for-civilians-in-Ukraine-since-2022-UN-human-rights-monitors-find). In the first half of 2026, civilian casualties climbed [another 37 percent](http://ukraine.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/2026-07/Ukraine%20-%20protection%20of%20civilians%20in%20armed%20conflict%20June%20and%20the%20first%20six%20months%20of%202026_ENG.pdf). In September, at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured — an 85 percent jump over the previous September. October is on pace to be [deadlier still](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168614).

Ms. Matviichuk said she feared even worse bloodshed as Mr. Trump openly sides with Russia, with Ukraine reporting sudden speed restrictions with a Pentagon-controlled satellite internet system, gaps in the sharing of U.S. military intelligence and delays in deliveries of interceptor missiles.

Mr. Trump has also demanded that Ukraine stop striking oil refineries, Kyiv’s best way to choke off funding for Russian attacks. While Mr. Trump has claimed that the strikes have raised diesel prices in the United States, energy experts say that the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran has played a larger role.

“When you take the resources that the defending side needs for its defense, you’re not stopping the war,” Ms. Matviichuk said.

Image

A diesel station in New York City last month. Energy experts say Mr. Trump’s decision to purchase Russian diesel in an effort to bring down fuel prices before the midterm elections will prove futile.Credit...Hilary Swift for The New York Times

While Mr. Trump accuses Mr. Zelensky of not wanting peace, Ukrainians say the question of why they are still fighting is as absurd as it is obvious: They have no choice.

Russia invaded Ukraine. Kyiv has agreed to Trump administration proposals to lower the violence, from a total cease-fire to limited truces on land, in the air and at sea. Moscow has agreed to none of any substance.

The Russian military is stockpiling hundreds of ballistic missiles, thousands of cruise missiles and tens of thousands of drones for a [winter campaign](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/world/europe/russia-ukraine-winter.html) aimed at rendering Ukrainian cities unlivable, [according to Ukrainian intelligence](https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2026/10/21/8058998/). Russia’s economy remains centered on war, and Mr. Putin has never backed down from his maximalist demands.
